title: Putting It Together: An Annotated Mock Interview
tagline: Watch the framework applied end to end on 'Design Pastebin' — with the reasoning narrated at every step.
summary: A full worked interview showing the framework in action.

paragraphs: Interviewer: 'Design Pastebin — a service where a user pastes text and gets a short URL others can use to read it.' Pastebin is a great teaching example: simple enough to cover fully in one lesson, yet it exercises every step of the framework. Watch how each phase flows into the next.
Throughout, italic notes explain *why* the candidate is doing each thing — that meta-reasoning is what you're learning to internalize.

blocks.text: Notice the very first move: the candidate does NOT start designing. They announce a plan and clarify scope. That single habit puts you ahead of most candidates immediately.

paragraphs: Candidate: 'Let me clarify scope first, then estimate, sketch the API and data model, draw a high-level design, and deep-dive the interesting parts.'

blocks.title: Functional (agreed)
items: Create a paste (text) and get back a unique short URL.
Read a paste via its URL.
Optional expiration (TTL) and custom alias. (Analytics, editing → out of scope.)

blocks.title: Non-functional (agreed)
items: Read-heavy (a paste is created once, read many times).
Pastes can be large-ish text (cap at, say, 10 MB).
Short URLs unique and not easily enumerable.

blocks.text: Why it matters: 'read-heavy' and 'pastes can be large' are the two observations that shape the entire design — caching for reads, and storing big blobs separately from metadata. The candidate surfaced both in the first two minutes.

The numbers are modest — the candidate notes this honestly: 'This isn't a huge-scale problem, so I won't over-engineer. A single primary DB with a replica and a cache handles this comfortably; I'll mention how it scales if reads grew 100×.' Matching complexity to scale is a senior signal.

codes.title: api

blocks.title: Data model — split metadata from the blob

items.detail: key (PK), createdAt, expireAt, contentLocation, size. Small, structured, queried by key.
The actual paste text goes in object storage (S3), keyed by the same id. Keeps large blobs out of the DB and is cheap + durable.

blocks.title: The metadata-DB pattern
blocks.text: Storing big content in blob storage and only a pointer + metadata in the database is a recurring pattern (same as the file-storage and video case studies). The candidate names it explicitly — pattern recognition reads as experience.

blocks.caption: Write stores blob + metadata; read is cache-first, falling through to DB + blob store.

items.title: Create (write)
items.detail: Service generates a unique key (base62 of a distributed id, or a pre-generated key from a key-gen service so it's non-enumerable), writes content to blob storage, writes metadata to the DB, returns the short URL.

items.title: Read
items.detail: Check Redis first → hit returns instantly. On miss, read metadata from DB, fetch content from blob storage, populate cache, return. Since it's read-heavy with a small hot set, cache hit rate is high.

blocks.text: Candidate pauses: 'Does this high-level design look reasonable before I go deeper?' — getting agreement before deep-diving is textbook framework discipline.

items.detail: 'A plain auto-increment is a bottleneck and enumerable. I'd base62-encode ids from a distributed generator, or use a key-generation service that pre-shuffles a pool of keys so they're unique and non-sequential.' (Ties directly to the URL-shortener case study.)
'Store expireAt; on read, return 410 if past it (lazy expiry). A background job (or the blob store's lifecycle policy + DB TTL) reclaims expired data so we don't leak storage.'
'It's a single hot read key — served straight from Redis/CDN, so the DB barely sees it. I'd watch for cache stampede if it expires: pin hot keys or serve-stale-while-revalidate.'

'Stateless app servers behind the LB, DB read replicas, shard metadata by key via consistent hashing, and the cache + a CDN for content absorb read growth. The cache is an optimization, not a SPOF — misses fall through to DB + blob store.'

blocks.text: Notice: the candidate deep-dives the genuinely hard/interesting parts (key generation, hot keys, failure) rather than re-explaining obvious boxes — and quantifies and trade-offs each. That's where senior signal is earned.

items.detail: Key generation (solved with distributed ids/key-gen), cache node failure (falls through), DB write throughput (modest here; shard if it grows).

Eventual consistency on the read path is fine (a paste never changes after creation, so cache staleness is a non-issue — a nice property to call out). Chose blob storage over DB blobs for cost/durability.
Cache hit rate, read/write latency p99, error rates, storage growth, expired-cleanup lag.
'We met read-heavy + low-latency reads via cache-first, high availability via replication and a cache that's not a SPOF, and non-enumerable keys via the key-gen approach.'

blocks.text: The strongest possible finish: explicitly map the final design back to the requirements you agreed at minute three. It closes the loop and shows everything you built was in service of the goal — exactly the structured, intentional impression you want to leave.

cheatsheet: Open by announcing your plan and clarifying scope — never start designing cold.
Surface the defining characteristics early (here: read-heavy + large blobs) — they shape everything.
Estimate, state assumptions aloud, and match complexity to scale (don't over-engineer modest load).
Split metadata (DB) from large content (blob storage) — a recurring, experience-signaling pattern.
Get agreement on the high-level design before deep-diving.
Deep-dive the genuinely hard parts (key generation, hot keys, expiry, failure) — quantify and trade-off each.
Finish by naming bottlenecks/trade-offs/monitoring and mapping the design back to the original requirements.

questions.prompt: Without looking back, walk through how you'd design Pastebin using the framework, hitting each step in order.
questions.hint: Requirements → estimation → API/data → high-level → deep dive → trade-offs.
answer: **Requirements:** clarify scope — create a paste and get a short URL, read by URL, optional TTL/custom alias; analytics/editing out of scope. Non-functional: read-heavy, highly available, low-latency reads, pastes up to ~10 MB, non-enumerable keys.
**Estimation:** assume ~1M pastes/day → ~10 writes/sec; 10:1 reads → ~100 reads/sec (peak ~300); ~3.6 TB/year. Note it's modest scale, so don't over-engineer.

**API & data model:** POST /pastes returns a short URL; GET /{key} returns content. Split storage: metadata (key, timestamps, expireAt, pointer) in a DB; the paste content in blob storage keyed by the same id.

**High-level design:** client → LB → stateless Paste Service → Redis cache → metadata DB + blob store. Write: generate a unique key, store blob + metadata. Read: cache-first, fall through to DB+blob on miss, then populate cache.

**Deep dives:** unique non-guessable keys via base62 of a distributed id or a key-generation service; lazy expiry (410 past expireAt) plus a cleanup job/lifecycle policy; hot viral paste served from cache/CDN with stampede protection; scale via read replicas, sharding by key, and a CDN.

**Trade-offs/wrap-up:** pastes are immutable so cache staleness is a non-issue (nice property); blob storage over DB blobs for cost/durability; monitor cache hit rate, p99 latency, storage growth, cleanup lag; map it all back to the agreed requirements (read-heavy + low-latency + HA + non-enumerable keys).
keyPoints: Hits all steps in order: requirements → estimation → API/data → high-level → deep dive → trade-offs
Read-heavy framing drives cache-first; metadata/blob split for large content
Deep-dives keys, expiry, hot keys, scaling — not obvious boxes
Closes by mapping the design back to requirements
followUps: How would the design change if pastes could be edited after creation?

questions.prompt: In this walkthrough, why is it a genuinely nice property that pastes are immutable after creation?
questions.hint: Think about what immutability does to caching and consistency.
answer: Because immutability makes the hard problem of cache consistency basically disappear. In most read-heavy systems, the tricky part of caching is invalidation: when the underlying data changes, the cached copy becomes stale and you need an invalidation or write-through strategy to avoid serving wrong data. But a paste never changes after it's created — the content is fixed for the life of the key. So once it's in the cache, the cached value can never be stale; there's nothing to invalidate.

That lets us cache aggressively and indefinitely (until expiry/eviction) with zero risk of serving incorrect data, push content to a CDN without worrying about purges on update, and avoid the complexity of write-through or invalidation logic entirely. It's worth explicitly calling this out in the interview because recognizing that a data property (immutability) simplifies the architecture is exactly the kind of insight that signals you understand *why* caching is normally hard — and that you're designing intentionally rather than bolting on a cache by reflex.
keyPoints: Immutability eliminates the cache-invalidation problem (no staleness possible)
Can cache/CDN aggressively and indefinitely with no purge-on-update logic
Calling it out signals you understand why caching is normally hard
followUps: What caching/invalidation complications reappear the moment you allow editing pastes?
